Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 81, verse 15–29:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So I swear by the receding stars﴾ — "lā" is extra (ṣila), and the meaning is: "I swear by al-khunnas." There are five opinions concerning them.

(p-42) The first: they are five stars that recede (takhnasu) during the day, so they are not seen. They are: Zuhal (Saturn), ʿUtarid (Mercury), al-Mushtari (Jupiter), al-Marrikh (Mars), and al-Zuhra (Venus). This was said by ʿAli, and Muqatil and Ibn Qutayba also held it. It was said: the name of Jupiter is al-Burjus, and the name of Mars is Bahram.

The second: they are the stars in general. This was said by al-Hasan and Qatada without restriction, and Abu ʿUbayda also held it.

The third: they are the wild oxen (baqar al-wahsh). This was said by Ibn Masʿud.

The fourth: they are the gazelles. It was related by al-ʿAwfi from Ibn ʿAbbas, and Saʿid ibn Jubayr also held it.

The fifth: they are the angels. This is related by al-Mawardi. Most scholars hold that they are the stars.

Ibn Qutayba said: He called them khunnas because they travel through the zodiac signs and the lunar mansions, like the movement of the sun and the moon, and then they recede (takhnas), i.e., return; whenever one of them is seen at the end of the zodiac signs, it turns back to its beginning. He called them kunnas because they hide (takbunu), i.e., they move as gazelles hide (takmus al-zibaʾ). Al-Zajjaj said: takhnas means they set (taghib), and likewise takmus means they set in the places where they set. If the intended meaning is the gazelles, then it means they enter the kunas, which is a branch of the branches of a tree. Yaʿqub read "al-jawari" with a yaʾ when pausing.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And by the night when it turns away﴾ — concerning it there are two opinions.

The first: it turns away (wallā). This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas, Ibn Zayd, and al-Farraʾ.
